## Teaching points

1. In ankylosing spondylitis the fused, osteoporotic spine breaks like a long bone: low-energy falls cause transverse, three-column (chalk-stick) fractures, most often at C6–C7, that are usually unstable.
2. NEXUS and the Canadian C-spine rule do not address or explicitly exclude ankylosing spondylitis: image every such patient with neck pain after trauma by CT, with a low threshold for MRI.
3. New neurological deficit after a fall in AS means spinal cord injury or epidural haematoma until proven otherwise, even when a stroke alert has been called; bilateral upper motor neuron signs with neck pain localise to the cervical cord.
4. Immobilise in the pre-injury (often kyphotic) alignment; forcing the neck straight into a standard collar can displace the fracture.
5. Instability, epidural haematoma or a deteriorating examination need urgent spinal surgery; haematomas can also appear hours after injury.
